# Preserved Directions {#preserved-directions}

Which lines through the origin does a matrix send into themselves?

- [An eigenvector stays on its own line](#an-eigenvector-stays-on-its-own-line)
- [Chosen directions reveal the action](#two-directions-reveal-the-action)
- [An eigenvalue describes a scalar action](#an-eigenvalue-describes-a-scalar-action)
- [Recognize eigenvectors before computing](#recognize-eigenvectors-before-computing)

## An eigenvector stays on its own line {#an-eigenvector-stays-on-its-own-line}

For a square matrix $\mat{A}$, an [eigenvector]{.alert} is a [nonzero]{.alert} vector $\vct{v}$ satisfying

$$
\mat{A}\vct{v}=\lambda\vct{v},\qquad \vct{v}\ne\vct{0}
$$

The scalar $\lambda$ is its [eigenvalue]{.alert}

- Every multiple of $\vct{v}$ is mapped into its span

\begin{equation*}
\mat{A}\operatorname{span}\{\vct{v}\}\subseteq\operatorname{span}\{\vct{v}\},
\qquad \text{equality when }\lambda\ne0
\end{equation*}

- A nonzero multiple is another eigenvector for the same eigenvalue
- The zero vector satisfies the equation for every $\lambda$, so it is excluded

::: {.key-point}
The line is preserved as a subspace; its vectors may stretch, reverse, or collapse
:::

::: {.notes}
A is n-by-n over a specified field, initially R. For any scalar c,
A(cv)=cAv=lambda(cv). When lambda=0 the entire line maps to zero, so
“preserved” means invariant (mapped into itself), not necessarily mapped onto
itself. A nonzero eigenvector can have zero entries. Zero is an allowed
eigenvalue, but the zero vector is never an eigenvector. The real/complex
field distinction becomes essential in the complex-eigenvalue section.
:::

## Chosen directions reveal the action {#two-directions-reveal-the-action}

$$
\mat{A}=\begin{bmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{bmatrix},\qquad
\vct{v}_1=\begin{bmatrix}1\\1\end{bmatrix},\quad
\vct{v}_2=\begin{bmatrix}1\\-1\end{bmatrix}
$$

![](assets/eigenvalues/eigen-directions.svg){fig-alt="Before and after applying A with rows 2,1 and 1,2. The vector v1=(1,1) becomes (3,3) on the same diagonal line; v2=(1,-1) stays fixed. The vector e1=(1,0) becomes (2,1), leaving its original line." width="70%" .nostretch}

$$
\mat{A}\vct{v}_1=3\vct{v}_1,\qquad
\mat{A}\vct{v}_2=\vct{v}_2
$$

::: {.key-point}
The standard axes mix; the two diagonal directions act independently
:::

## An eigenvalue describes a scalar action {#an-eigenvalue-describes-a-scalar-action}

For a real eigenvalue and its eigenvector:

| Eigenvalue | Action on that vector |
|---|---|
| $\lambda>1$ | stretch in the same direction |
| $0<\lambda<1$ | shrink in the same direction |
| $\lambda=1$ | leave fixed |
| $\lambda<0$ | reverse direction and scale length by $|\lambda|$ |
| $\lambda=0$ | send to zero |

For a square matrix,

$$
0\text{ is an eigenvalue}\iff\operatorname{null}(\mat{A})\ne\{\vct{0}\}
\iff\mat{A}\text{ is singular}
$$

::: {.key-point}
The scale factor belongs to a direction; it need not describe every vector
:::

## Recognize eigenvectors before computing {#recognize-eigenvectors-before-computing}

::: {.exitem .lettered}
<span class="exbullet">$\exstar$</span>
<span>Find eigenvalues and describe their eigendirections geometrically
<span class="exsub">Reflection $\mat{H}=\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{bmatrix}$</span>
<span class="exsub">Projection $\mat{J}=\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\0&0\end{bmatrix}$</span>
<span class="exsub">Scaling $\mat{S}=2\mat{I}_2$: which nonzero vectors are eigenvectors?</span>
<span class="exsub">For the preceding $\mat{A}=\begin{bmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{bmatrix}$, is $[2,1]^\top$ an eigenvector?</span>
</span>
:::

::: {.notes}
H: eigenvalue 1 on the horizontal axis, -1 on the vertical axis. J:
eigenvalue 1 on the horizontal axis, 0 on the vertical axis. S: every
nonzero vector has eigenvalue 2. For A, A[2,1]^T=[5,4]^T, which is not
a scalar multiple of [2,1]^T. These are all the real eigenvalues for the
first three matrices. Reconnect H and J to Matrix Transformations.
:::

# Eigenvalues and Eigenspaces {#eigenvalues-and-eigenspaces}

Turn the preserved-direction question into a homogeneous system

- [A nonzero null vector identifies an eigenvalue](#a-nonzero-null-vector-identifies-an-eigenvalue)
- [Example: find eigenvalues, then eigenvectors](#find-eigenvalues-then-eigenvectors)
- [An eigenspace includes all vectors for one eigenvalue](#an-eigenspace-includes-all-vectors-for-one-eigenvalue)
- [Example: a spinning tennis racket](#a-spinning-tennis-racket)
- [Compute and check an eigenspace](#compute-and-check-an-eigenspace)
- [Trace and determinant check the eigenvalues](#trace-and-determinant-check-the-eigenvalues)
- [Use software for practical eigenvalue problems](#use-software-for-practical-eigenvalue-problems)

## A nonzero null vector identifies an eigenvalue {#a-nonzero-null-vector-identifies-an-eigenvalue}

For $\mat{A}\in\reals^{n\times n}$ and $\vct{v}\ne\vct{0}$:

$$
\mat{A}\vct{v}=\lambda\vct{v}
\iff(\mat{A}-\lambda\mat{I}_n)\vct{v}=\vct{0}
\iff\vct{0}\ne\vct{v}\in\nullspace(\mat{A}-\lambda\mat{I}_n)
$$

A nonzero solution exists exactly when the shifted matrix is singular:

$$
\det(\mat{A}-\lambda\mat{I}_n)=0
$$

Define the [characteristic polynomial]{.alert}

$$
p_{\mat{A}}(\lambda)=\det(\lambda\mat{I}_n-\mat{A})
$$

Some sources use $\det(\mat{A}-\lambda\mat{I}_n)$ — the same roots and multiplicities

::: {.key-point}
First solve the scalar polynomial equation; then solve a homogeneous system for each root
:::

::: {.notes}
We follow Anton's monic convention det(lambda I-A), with leading coefficient
1 and constant term (-1)^n det(A). The alternative det(A-lambda I) differs
by (-1)^n and has exactly the same roots with the same multiplicities.
The two polynomials agree in even dimensions and have opposite signs in odd
dimensions. A characteristic equation may be multiplied by a nonzero
constant without changing its solutions.
The equivalence uses the invertibility/determinant results already taught.
To find eigenvectors after finding a root, reduce A-lambda I and solve its
homogeneous system. A root guarantees at least one free variable, not a
unique eigenvector. Never divide a vector equation by a vector.
:::

## Example: find eigenvalues, then eigenvectors {#find-eigenvalues-then-eigenvectors}

Return to $\mat{A}=\begin{bmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{bmatrix}$

$$
p_{\mat{A}}(\lambda)
=\det\begin{bmatrix}\lambda-2&-1\\-1&\lambda-2\end{bmatrix}
=(\lambda-2)^2-1=(\lambda-3)(\lambda-1)
$$

For each eigenvalue, solve a different homogeneous system:

| $\lambda$ | $\mat{A}-\lambda\mat{I}$ | Solution condition | Eigenspace basis |
|---|---|---|---|
| $3$ | $\begin{bmatrix}-1&1\\1&-1\end{bmatrix}$ | $v_2=v_1$ | $\{[1,1]^\top\}$ |
| $1$ | $\begin{bmatrix}1&1\\1&1\end{bmatrix}$ | $v_2=-v_1$ | $\{[1,-1]^\top\}$ |

::: {.key-point}
The determinant finds the scale factors; null spaces find their directions
:::

::: {.notes}
Teaching reminder for the November 12 recap: correct the earlier general
square-matrix condition-number claim. The 2-norm condition number uses the
largest/smallest singular values, including for square matrices. This
example is symmetric positive definite, so its singular values equal its
positive eigenvalues and kappa(A)=3/1=3 is valid. Do not extend that eigenvalue
ratio to an arbitrary square matrix. Use kappa without a norm subscript.
:::

## An eigenspace includes all vectors for one eigenvalue {#an-eigenspace-includes-all-vectors-for-one-eigenvalue}

For an eigenvalue $\lambda$, its [eigenspace]{.alert} is

$$
E_\lambda=\operatorname{null}(\mat{A}-\lambda\mat{I})
$$

- It is a subspace: zero and all linear combinations remain in it
- Its nonzero vectors are exactly the eigenvectors with eigenvalue $\lambda$
- Its basis comes from [free variables]({{< meta decks.d01.file >}}#pivots-organize-elimination) in the shifted system

By [rank–nullity]({{< meta decks.d08.file >}}#rank-nullity-counts-inputs),

$$
\dim(E_\lambda)=n-\operatorname{rank}(\mat{A}-\lambda\mat{I})\ge1
$$

::: {.key-point}
Eigenvectors exclude zero; the eigenspace includes zero
:::

## Example: a spinning tennis racket {#a-spinning-tennis-racket}

The [inertia tensor]{.alert} $\mat{J}=\mat{J}^\top\in\reals^{3\times3}$ describes rotational inertia about the center of mass

\begin{equation*}
\mat{J}\vct{v}_j=I_j\vct{v}_j,\qquad 0<I_1<I_2<I_3
\end{equation*}

- Principal-axis directions $\vct{v}_j$: [eigenvectors]{.alert}; principal moments $I_j$: [eigenvalues]{.alert}
- Each eigenspace is a line: $E_{I_j}=\operatorname{span}\{\vct{v}_j\}$

| Axis through the center of mass | Moment | Rotation without external torque |
|---|---|---|
| Along the handle | Smallest | Stable |
| Across the racket, in its plane | Intermediate | Unstable |
| Perpendicular to the racket face | Largest | Stable |

::: {.key-point}
Rotation about the intermediate axis is possible, but small disturbances grow and make the racket tumble
:::

::: {.notes}
Demonstration: mark one face of the racket, compare tosses about the three
principal axes, and watch the extra face flip for the intermediate-axis toss.
Treat the racket as a rigid, approximately symmetric flat body. All axes pass
through its center of mass, and external torque about that point is neglected.
The tensor maps angular velocity to angular momentum; principal-axis rotation
makes those vectors parallel. The tensor is not the matrix of a spatial
rotation. Its three distinct principal moments make these eigenspaces
one-dimensional. Exact steady rotation about the intermediate axis is a valid
motion; instability means small off-axis disturbances grow, not that the
motion is impossible. The stability assertion is a result of rigid-body
dynamics, not a consequence of the eigenvalue definition alone.

Sources: [UT Austin: principal axes of rotation](https://farside.ph.utexas.edu/teaching/336k/lectures/node67.html)
and [Harvard: tennis racquet flip](https://sciencedemonstrations.fas.harvard.edu/presentations/tennis-racquet-flip).
:::

---

### A small wobble may oscillate or grow {#tennis-racket-wobble-eigenvalues}

Perfect spin about any principal axis is possible — test it with a tiny wobble

Let $\vct{u}$ contain the two small angular-velocity components perpendicular to the spin axis

The linear approximation uses a [different matrix]{.alert}, $\mat{B}$

$$
\vct{u}'=\mat{B}\vct{u},\qquad
\mat{B}\vct{w}=\mu\vct{w}
\implies \vct{u}(t)=e^{\mu t}\vct{w}
$$

| Steady spin axis | Wobble eigenvalues | Effect of a small disturbance |
|---|---|---|
| Smallest or largest moment | $\pm\sqrt{-1}\,\nu$ | Oscillation; wobble stays small |
| Intermediate moment | $\pm\sigma$ | A growing component; onset of tumbling |

$\nu,\sigma>0$ — imaginary rates oscillate; a positive real rate grows initially

::: {.key-point}
Inertia eigenvalues are principal moments; wobble eigenvalues govern growth or oscillation
:::

::: {.notes}
Keep the distinction verbal and brief: the inertia eigenvectors are the
natural spin axes, and the three positive inertia eigenvalues are the
principal moments. Perfect torque-free spin about any one axis is possible.
The new question is whether a tiny off-axis wobble stays small. The angular
velocity components are measured in the body-fixed principal-axis frame.
B is the two-dimensional transverse linearization about that chosen steady spin,
not the inertia tensor J. An eigenvector mode in the linear model evolves
as exp(mu t)w; its real and imaginary parts give real oscillatory solutions
when mu is purely imaginary. The displayed mode has initial data w, and
general small disturbances combine the two modes.
For the smallest and largest moments the pair is purely imaginary, giving
neutral oscillation, not decay back to the exact spin. For the middle moment
there is one positive and one negative real rate; a generic perturbation
contains the growing mode. The full three-component angular-velocity
linearization also has a zero eigenvalue, corresponding to changing the
steady spin speed along the same axis. It is omitted because u contains
only the two perpendicular components.
Assume a rigid body, no external torque, three distinct principal moments
and nonzero spin. Conserved energy and angular-momentum magnitude support
the bounded-wobble interpretation at the extreme axes; imaginary eigenvalues
alone do not prove nonlinear stability for every system. Intermediate-axis
growth describes the initial small disturbance; the full motion remains
energy bounded and develops into tumbling rather than unbounded spin speed.
Optional physical intuition: at fixed angular-momentum magnitude, the energy
has extrema at the extreme-moment axes and a saddle at the middle axis.
Nearby conserved-energy contours surround the extrema but allow departures
near the saddle. No Euler-equation derivation is needed for this illustration.

Source: [TU Delft: Euler's equations and the tennis racket theorem](https://interactivetextbooks.tudelft.nl/nb1140/content/generalrotationalmotion.html#euler-s-equations).
:::

## Compute and check an eigenspace {#compute-and-check-an-eigenspace}

$$
\mat{B}=\begin{bmatrix}4&1\\0&2\end{bmatrix}
$$

::: {.exitem .lettered}
<span class="exbullet">$\exstar$</span>
<span>Use determinants, homogeneous systems, and direct multiplication
<span class="exsub">Find the characteristic polynomial and both eigenvalues</span>
<span class="exsub">Find a basis for each eigenspace</span>
<span class="exsub">Check $\mat{B}\vct{v}=\lambda\vct{v}$ for each chosen basis vector</span>
<span class="exsub">Does $\vct{e}_2$ have to be an eigenvector because $\mat{B}$ is triangular?</span>
</span>
:::

::: {.notes}
p_B=(lambda-4)(lambda-2). E_4=span{[1,0]^T}; E_2=span{[1,-2]^T}.
B[1,-2]^T=[2,-4]^T=2[1,-2]^T. B e2=[1,2]^T, not a multiple
of e2. Triangular diagonal entries give eigenvalues, not necessarily
standard-basis eigenvectors. The two chosen eigenvectors are independent.
:::

## Trace and determinant check the eigenvalues {#trace-and-determinant-check-the-eigenvalues}

Count all $n$ eigenvalues with algebraic multiplicity, allowing complex roots

$$
\operatorname{tr}(\mat{A})=\sum_{j=1}^n\lambda_j,
\qquad \det(\mat{A})=\prod_{j=1}^n\lambda_j
$$

For $\mat{A}=\begin{bmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{bmatrix}$:
$\quad3+1=4$, $\quad3\cdot1=3$

For any triangular matrix, the characteristic determinant is a product:

$$
p_{\mat{U}}(\lambda)=\prod_{j=1}^n(\lambda-u_{jj})
$$

::: {.key-point}
Triangular eigenvalues are the diagonal entries; trace and determinant are checks, not a general eigensolver
:::

::: {.notes}
The coefficient of lambda^(n-1) in the monic characteristic polynomial is
-tr(A); its constant coefficient is (-1)^n det(A). Comparing with the
factored polynomial proves both identities, without diagonalizability.
The identities do not generally determine all eigenvalues when n>2.
For a triangular matrix, lambda I-U remains triangular, so its determinant
is the product of its diagonal entries. A real matrix may have nonreal roots;
that topic is developed below rather than excluded by the real entries.
:::

## Use software for practical eigenvalue problems {#use-software-for-practical-eigenvalue-problems}

Hand calculations reveal the ideas; software handles practical matrix sizes

- Diagonal or triangular matrices: read eigenvalues from the diagonal
- General matrices: use an eigenvalue solver rather than expand a characteristic determinant
- Python: `numpy.linalg.eig(A)`; for real symmetric matrices, `numpy.linalg.eigh(A)`

For a computed eigenpair, check

\begin{equation*}
\mat{A}\widehat{\vct{v}}\approx\widehat{\lambda}\widehat{\vct{v}},
\qquad \widehat{\vct{v}}\ne\vct{0}
\end{equation*}

::: {.key-point}
Understand the eigenvalue equation and interpret the directions; let software do the larger computations
:::

::: {.notes}
The characteristic polynomial defines the eigenvalues, but numerical eigensolvers
normally work directly with the matrix rather than expand that polynomial and
find its roots. Use small or structured examples for exact hand calculations.
Once an exact eigenvalue is known, row reduction of A-lambda I finds its
eigenspace. Row reduction of A itself does not preserve its eigenvalues.
Numerical eigenvectors are approximate and may be rescaled or reordered;
check the corresponding eigenvalue/vector pair together. Interpret the residual
relative to the scales of A and v. A small residual alone does not guarantee
small forward errors for a sensitive nonsymmetric eigenvalue problem.
The companion demonstrates eigh, residual checks and orthonormality.
:::

# Eigenvector Bases and Diagonalization {#eigenvector-bases-and-diagonalization}

When do preserved directions provide enough coordinates for every vector?

- [An eigenvector basis makes the matrix diagonal](#an-eigenvector-basis-makes-the-matrix-diagonal)
- [Repeated roots may leave too few directions](#repeated-roots-may-leave-too-few-directions)
- [A diagonalization recipe](#a-diagonalization-recipe)
- [Optional: generalized eigenvectors](#optional-generalized-eigenvectors)
- [Similarity changes coordinates, not the operator](#similarity-changes-coordinates-not-the-operator)

## An eigenvector basis makes the matrix diagonal {#an-eigenvector-basis-makes-the-matrix-diagonal}

For the ordered eigenbasis $\mathcal{V}=\{\vct{v}_1,\ldots,\vct{v}_n\}$,
match each column to its eigenvalue

$$
\mat{V}=[\vct{v}_1\ \cdots\ \vct{v}_n],\qquad
\mat{D}=\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_n)
$$

Multiplication by columns gives

$$
\mat{A}\mat{V}=[\lambda_1\vct{v}_1\ \cdots\ \lambda_n\vct{v}_n]
=\mat{V}\mat{D}
$$

Independence makes $\mat{V}$ invertible:

$$
\boxed{\mat{V}^{-1}\mat{A}\mat{V}=\mat{D}},\qquad
\mat{A}=\mat{V}\mat{D}\mat{V}^{-1}
$$

::: {.key-point}
$\mat{A}$ is [diagonalizable]{.alert} over the chosen field exactly when it has an eigenvector basis there
:::

::: {.notes}
The converse is equally important. If V^{-1} A V=D is diagonal and V is
invertible, multiply by V to obtain AV=VD. Column j says A v_j=lambda_j v_j.
The columns of invertible V form a basis, so this is an eigenvector basis.
The order of eigenvalues must match the order of columns. Scaling a column
by a nonzero constant gives another valid V with the same D. A matrix with
an eigenvalue zero may still be diagonalizable; V, not D, must be invertible.
:::

---

### Example: diagonalize and read the coordinates {#diagonalize-and-read-the-coordinates}

For $\mat{A}=\begin{bmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{bmatrix}$, choose

$$
\mat{V}=\begin{bmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{bmatrix},\qquad
\mat{V}^{-1}=\tfrac12\begin{bmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{bmatrix},\qquad
\mat{D}=\begin{bmatrix}3&0\\0&1\end{bmatrix}
$$

For $\vct{x}=[4,2]^\top$, write $\vct{c}=[\vct{x}]_{\mathcal{V}}=\mat{V}^{-1}\vct{x}$

$$
\mat{A}\vct{x}=\begin{bmatrix}10\\8\end{bmatrix}
\quad\xleftarrow{\mat{V}}\quad
\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}9\\1\end{bmatrix}}_{[\mat{A}\vct{x}]_{\mathcal{V}}}
\quad\xleftarrow{\mat{D}}\quad
\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}3\\1\end{bmatrix}}_{[\vct{x}]_{\mathcal{V}}}
$$

::: {.key-point}
Read coordinates, scale them separately, then reconstruct the output
:::

::: {.notes}
Check V D V^{-1}=A and V^{-1}V=I. The input x is 3v1+v2; the output
is 9v1+v2. Direct multiplication gives [10,8]^T. V maps eigenbasis
coordinates to standard coordinates; V^{-1} goes the reverse way.
This is the same coordinate route taught in Bases and Coordinates.
:::

---

### Diagonalization is a change of coordinates {#diagonalization-is-a-change-of-coordinates}

Use the inverse basis matrix as in
[{{< meta decks.d07.short_title >}}]({{< meta decks.d07.file >}}#a-basis-matrix-converts-coordinates-to-standard-form)

::: {.eigen-map role="group" aria-label="Read from right to left: the basis matrix V maps the eigenbasis coordinate column c in the right box to the vector x in the left box. Its inverse reads those coordinates."}
<div class="diagram-node eigen-map-input">
<span class="diagram-label">Eigenbasis coordinates</span>
<span class="eigen-map-line">$[\vct{x}]_{\mathcal{V}}=\vct{c}=\begin{bmatrix}c_1\\\vdots\\c_n\end{bmatrix}$</span>
</div>
<div class="diagram-arrow eigen-map-arrow">$\xleftarrow{\quad\mat{V}\quad}$</div>
<div class="diagram-node eigen-map-output">
<span class="diagram-label">Vector</span>
<span class="eigen-map-line">$\displaystyle\vct{x}=\sum_{j=1}^n c_j\vct{v}_j$</span>
<span class="eigen-map-line">$\vct{x}=\mat{V}\vct{c}$</span>
</div>
:::

Apply $\mat{A}$ to the vector or $\mat{D}$ to its eigenbasis coordinates

$$
\mat{A}\vct{x}=\mat{A}(\mat{V}\vct{c})=\mat{V}(\mat{D}\vct{c}),
\qquad [\mat{A}\vct{x}]_{\mathcal{V}}=\mat{D}[\vct{x}]_{\mathcal{V}}
$$

$\mat{V}^{-1}$ reads the coordinates; $\mat{D}$ scales them separately

::: {.key-point}
The operator is unchanged; the new coordinates separate its scalar actions
:::

::: {.notes}
Recall the coordinate-to-vector boxes from Bases and Coordinates. The right
box contains the eigenbasis coordinate column; the left box contains the
vector described in standard coordinates. The scalar field is real or
complex, as specified for the chosen eigenbasis. AV=VD says that building
the vector then applying A agrees with applying D to its coordinates then
building the output vector.
The basis may be oblique or scaled; V need not preserve lengths or angles.
For the preceding example, c=[3,1]^T and Dc=[9,1]^T; V sends these to
x=[4,2]^T and Ax=[10,8]^T. Later replace the single action D by e^(tD):
the same coordinate change will separate an entire differential system.
:::

---

### Example: two descriptions of one action {#two-descriptions-of-one-action}

Use an eigenbasis whose vectors are not perpendicular:

$$
\mat{B}=\begin{bmatrix}4&1\\0&2\end{bmatrix},\qquad
\mat{V}=\begin{bmatrix}1&1\\0&-2\end{bmatrix},\qquad
\mat{D}=\begin{bmatrix}4&0\\0&2\end{bmatrix}
$$

$\mat{B}\mat{V}=\mat{V}\mat{D}$; start with $\vct{x}=[3,-2]^\top$

::: {.eigen-map .eigen-map-square role="group" aria-label="A commuting square with eigenbasis coordinate columns on the right and corresponding vectors on the left. Read horizontal arrows right to left: V maps c=(2,1) to x=(3,-2). Downward D on the right maps c to (8,2), while downward B on the left maps x to (10,-4). V also maps the lower coordinate column to the lower vector."}
<div class="diagram-node eigen-map-input">
<span class="diagram-label">Eigenbasis coordinates</span>
<span class="eigen-map-line">$[\vct{x}]_{\mathcal{V}}=\vct{c}=\begin{bmatrix}2\\1\end{bmatrix}$</span>
</div>
<div class="diagram-arrow eigen-map-arrow">$\xleftarrow{\quad\mat{V}\quad}$</div>
<div class="diagram-node eigen-map-output">
<span class="diagram-label">Vector</span>
<span class="eigen-map-line">$\vct{x}=\mat{V}\vct{c}=\begin{bmatrix}3\\-2\end{bmatrix}$</span>
</div>
<div class="diagram-arrow eigen-map-coordinate-action">$\mat{D}\big\downarrow$</div>
<div class="diagram-arrow eigen-map-vector-action">$\mat{B}\big\downarrow$</div>
<div class="diagram-node eigen-map-lower-input">
<span class="diagram-label">Coordinates after the action</span>
<span class="eigen-map-line">$[\mat{B}\vct{x}]_{\mathcal{V}}=\mat{D}\vct{c}=\begin{bmatrix}8\\2\end{bmatrix}$</span>
</div>
<div class="diagram-arrow eigen-map-lower-arrow">$\xleftarrow{\quad\mat{V}\quad}$</div>
<div class="diagram-node eigen-map-lower-output">
<span class="diagram-label">Output vector</span>
<span class="eigen-map-line">$\mat{B}\vct{x}=\mat{V}\mat{D}\vct{c}=\begin{bmatrix}10\\-4\end{bmatrix}$</span>
</div>
:::

::: {.key-point}
Across then down equals down then across: $\mat{B}(\mat{V}\vct{c})=\mat{V}(\mat{D}\vct{c})$
:::

::: {.notes}
The eigenbasis is v1=[1,0]^T for lambda1=4 and v2=[1,-2]^T for lambda2=2.
These are the eigenvectors found in the earlier triangular-matrix exercise.
They are independent but not perpendicular. Direct multiplication gives
BV=VD=[[4,2],[0,-4]]. Solve Vc=x: -2c2=-2 gives c2=1, then
c1+c2=3 gives c1=2. Equivalently V^{-1}=[[1,1/2],[0,-1/2]].
The upper coordinate column builds x=2v1+v2=[3,-2]^T. D multiplies
the two coefficients by 4 and 2, producing 8v1+2v2=[10,-4]^T.
Directly Bx=[4*3-2,2*(-2)]^T=[10,-4]^T. The vertical arrows apply the
same operator in the two coordinate systems; horizontal V changes the
description. This is not an orthogonal coordinate change: V need not preserve
Euclidean lengths or angles. Keep x distinct from its eigenbasis column c.
:::

---

### Practice changing to eigenbasis coordinates {#practice-changing-to-eigenbasis-coordinates}

Use the same $\mat{B},\mat{V},\mat{D}$, now with $\vct{x}=[1,2]^\top$

::: {.eigen-map role="group" aria-label="Find the unknown eigenbasis coordinates c1 and c2 in the right box. Read the map V from right to left: it sends their column to x=(1,2) in the left box."}
<div class="diagram-node eigen-map-input">
<span class="diagram-label">Find these coordinates</span>
<span class="eigen-map-line">$\vct{c}=[\vct{x}]_{\mathcal{V}}=\begin{bmatrix}c_1\\c_2\end{bmatrix}$</span>
</div>
<div class="diagram-arrow eigen-map-arrow">$\xleftarrow{\quad\mat{V}\quad}$</div>
<div class="diagram-node eigen-map-output">
<span class="diagram-label">Given vector</span>
<span class="eigen-map-line">$\vct{x}=\begin{bmatrix}1\\2\end{bmatrix}$</span>
</div>
:::

::: {.exitem .lettered}
<span class="exbullet">$\exstar$</span>
<span>Complete the coordinate route
<span class="exsub">Find $\vct{c}$ and write $\vct{x}=c_1\vct{v}_1+c_2\vct{v}_2$</span>
<span class="exsub">Use $\mat{D}\vct{c}$ to find $[\mat{B}\vct{x}]_{\mathcal{V}}$, then reconstruct $\mat{B}\vct{x}$ and check by direct multiplication</span>
<span class="exsub">Compute $\mat{D}\vct{x}$; does it equal $\mat{B}\vct{x}$? Which coordinate column should $\mat{D}$ act on?</span>
</span>
:::

::: {.notes}
Vc=x gives -2c2=2 and c1+c2=1, so c=[2,-1]^T.
Thus x=2v1-v2. Dc=[8,-2]^T, and V(Dc)=8v1-2v2=[6,4]^T.
Directly Bx=[4*1+2,2*2]^T=[6,4]^T. But Dx=[4,4]^T differs.
Multiplying D by the standard-coordinate column x is a defined matrix
product, but it does not represent B's action on that vector. D represents
the operator on eigenbasis coordinates, so apply it to c=V^{-1}x and use V
to reconstruct the output. The same matrices and eigenvalue-column order
from the preceding example are used throughout this exercise.
:::

---

### Distinct eigenvalues supply independent eigenvectors {#distinct-eigenvalues-supply-independent-eigenvectors}

Eigenvectors belonging to distinct eigenvalues are linearly independent

For two eigenvectors, suppose $c_1\vct{v}_1+c_2\vct{v}_2=\vct{0}$

Apply $\mat{A}$, then substitute $c_2\vct{v}_2=-c_1\vct{v}_1$ from the original relation

\begin{align*}
\vct{0}&=c_1\lambda_1\vct{v}_1+\lambda_2(c_2\vct{v}_2)\\
&=c_1\lambda_1\vct{v}_1-\lambda_2 c_1\vct{v}_1\\
&=c_1(\lambda_1-\lambda_2)\vct{v}_1
\end{align*}

Since $\lambda_1\ne\lambda_2$ and $\vct{v}_1\ne\vct{0}$, $c_1=0$, then $c_2=0$

For $k$ eigenvectors, eliminate the last term as above and apply induction to the first $k-1$

::: {.key-point}
An $n\times n$ matrix with $n$ distinct eigenvalues in the chosen field is diagonalizable there
:::

::: {.notes}
The one-vector case holds because an eigenvector is nonzero. For k distinct
eigenvalues, start with a zero relation among v1,...,vk, apply A, and use the
original relation to substitute for c_k v_k in the term lambda_k(c_k v_k).
The remaining k-1 terms have coefficients c_j(lambda_j-lambda_k). By
induction the first k-1 vectors are independent, so those coefficients vanish.
Distinct eigenvalues give c_j=0 for j<k. The original relation then gives
c_k=0 since v_k is nonzero. The identity matrix shows that diagonalizability
can also hold with repeated eigenvalues.
:::

## Repeated roots may leave too few directions {#repeated-roots-may-leave-too-few-directions}

Two matrices with the same characteristic polynomial $(\lambda-2)^2$:

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="47%"}
$$
\mat{S}=\begin{bmatrix}2&0\\0&2\end{bmatrix}
$$

$\mat{S}-2\mat{I}=\mat{0}$

$E_2=\reals^2$: two independent eigenvectors

[Diagonalizable]{.alert}
:::
::: {.column width="6%"}
:::
::: {.column width="47%"}
$$
\mat{J}=\begin{bmatrix}2&1\\0&2\end{bmatrix}
$$

$\mat{J}-2\mat{I}=\begin{bmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{bmatrix}$

$E_2=\operatorname{span}\{\vct{e}_1\}$: only one independent eigenvector

[Not diagonalizable]{.alert}
:::
:::

::: {.key-point}
Repeated roots permit diagonalization, but do not guarantee enough eigenvectors
:::

---

### Count eigenspace dimensions before building a basis {#count-eigenspace-dimensions-before-building-a-basis}

For each eigenvalue $\lambda$:

| Multiplicity | What it counts |
|---|---|
| [Algebraic]{.alert}, $a_\lambda$ | repetitions of the root in $p_{\mat{A}}$ |
| [Geometric]{.alert}, $g_\lambda$ | $\dim(E_\lambda)$: independent eigenvectors available |

$$
1\le g_\lambda\le a_\lambda
$$

Over a field in which $p_{\mat{A}}$ splits into linear factors:

$$
\mat{A}\text{ diagonalizable}
\iff\sum_{\text{distinct }\lambda}g_\lambda=n
\iff g_\lambda=a_\lambda\text{ for every }\lambda
$$

::: {.key-point}
Collect a basis of each eigenspace; diagonalization needs $n$ independent columns altogether
:::

::: {.notes}
For a real eigenbasis all roots must be real. Over C the characteristic
polynomial always splits. To justify g<=a, extend a basis of E_lambda to
one of the whole space. In that basis A has block form
[[lambda I_g, B],[0,C]], whose characteristic polynomial contains
(t-lambda)^g. Thus g<=a. Eigenspaces for distinct eigenvalues form a direct
sum: apply the distinct-eigenvalue independence argument to a relation
among nonzero vectors, one from each eigenspace. Combining bases of the
individual eigenspaces is therefore independent. Since sum a=n when the
polynomial splits, the three displayed conditions are equivalent. A
repeated root is a prompt to compute nullity, not evidence of failure.
:::

## A diagonalization recipe {#a-diagonalization-recipe}

For a square matrix over the chosen field:

1. Factor $p_{\mat{A}}(\lambda)$ and list its distinct roots and multiplicities
2. For each root, solve $(\mat{A}-\lambda\mat{I})\vct{v}=\vct{0}$ and find an eigenspace basis
3. Count all independent eigenvectors obtained; fewer than $n$ means no eigenvector basis
4. If there are $n$, put them into $\mat{V}$ and their matching eigenvalues into $\mat{D}$
5. Check $\mat{A}\mat{V}=\mat{V}\mat{D}$ and that $\mat{V}$ is invertible

::: {.key-point}
If the characteristic polynomial does not split in the field, diagonalization there is impossible

&nbsp;

Verification by $\mat{A}\mat{V}=\mat{V}\mat{D}$ avoids computing an inverse
:::

---

### Practice deciding whether diagonalization is possible {#practice-deciding-whether-diagonalization-is-possible}

$$
\mat{B}=\begin{bmatrix}4&1\\0&2\end{bmatrix},\qquad
\mat{C}=\begin{bmatrix}2&0&0\\0&2&0\\0&0&3\end{bmatrix}
$$

::: {.exitem .lettered}
<span class="exbullet">$\exstar$</span>
<span>Build and verify eigenvector bases
<span class="exsub">Use the eigenspaces already found for $\mat{B}$ to construct $\mat{V},\mat{D}$; verify $\mat{B}\mat{V}=\mat{V}\mat{D}$</span>
<span class="exsub">For $\mat{C}$, give both multiplicities for each eigenvalue and construct an eigenvector basis</span>
<span class="exsub">Explain why $\mat{C}$ disproves “diagonalizable means all eigenvalues are distinct”</span>
</span>
:::

::: {.notes}
For B use V=[[1,1],[0,-2]], D=diag(4,2), V^{-1}=[[1,1/2],[0,-1/2]].
Both sides BV=VD=[[4,2],[0,-4]]. For C, lambda=2 has algebraic and
geometric multiplicity 2, E_2=span{e1,e2}; lambda=3 has both
multiplicities 1, E_3=span{e3}. V=I_3, D=C is a diagonalization.
Any basis within E_2 works, together with a nonzero vector from E_3.
:::

### A repeated-root test {#a-repeated-root-test}

$$
\mat{F}=\begin{bmatrix}2&1&0\\0&2&0\\0&0&3\end{bmatrix}
$$

::: {.exitem .lettered}
<span class="exbullet">$\exstar$</span>
<span>The diagonal entries give eigenvalues 2 and 3
<span class="exsub">Find the algebraic multiplicity and an eigenspace basis for each</span>
<span class="exsub">How many independent eigenvectors are available altogether?</span>
<span class="exsub">Can a different choice of vectors inside those same eigenspaces produce an eigenvector basis?</span>
</span>
:::

::: {.notes}
For lambda=2, F-2I has rows [0,1,0], [0,0,0], [0,0,1], so
E_2=span{e1}, algebraic multiplicity 2, geometric multiplicity 1.
For lambda=3, F-3I has rows [-1,1,0], [0,-1,0], [0,0,0], so
E_3=span{e3}, with both multiplicities 1. Only two independent
eigenvectors are available in dimension three. No change of basis within
these eigenspaces can increase their dimensions, so F is not diagonalizable.
:::

## Optional: generalized eigenvectors {#optional-generalized-eigenvectors}

Optional enrichment; may be skipped

Let $\lambda$ be a characteristic root of [algebraic multiplicity]{.alert} $k$

Its [generalized eigenspace]{.alert} is

$$
G_\lambda=\nullspace\bigl((\mat{A}-\lambda\mat{I}_n)^k\bigr),\qquad
E_\lambda=\nullspace(\mat{A}-\lambda\mat{I}_n)\subseteq G_\lambda
$$

A [generalized eigenvector]{.alert} is any nonzero vector in $G_\lambda$

Ordinary eigenvectors are included; a new direction lies in $G_\lambda\setminus E_\lambda$

A length-two [chain]{.alert} satisfies

$$
(\mat{A}-\lambda\mat{I})\vct{v}=\vct{0},\qquad
(\mat{A}-\lambda\mat{I})\vct{w}=\vct{v}\ne\vct{0}
$$

::: {.key-point}
$\mat{A}\vct{v}=\lambda\vct{v}$, but $\mat{A}\vct{w}=\lambda\vct{w}+\vct{v}$

The second direction feeds into the first instead of scaling independently
:::

::: {.notes}
This is optional enrichment, not a commitment to a Jordan algorithm.
Here k is the algebraic multiplicity of this eigenvalue: it is a sufficient
power for the whole generalized eigenspace, not necessarily the smallest
power that kills a particular vector. The original definition using some
positive integer power is equivalent to membership in this G_lambda.
Ordinary eigenvectors satisfy every positive-power condition; taking a
power greater than one alone does not exclude them. New generalized
directions are the vectors in G_lambda outside E_lambda. In the displayed
length-two chain, w is not an ordinary eigenvector because (A-lambda I)w
is nonzero, but (A-lambda I)^2 w=0. The vectors v,w are independent:
apply A-lambda I to av+bw=0 to obtain bv=0, hence b=0 and then a=0.
Use G for this generalized basis, V for a basis of ordinary eigenvectors,
and Q for an orthonormal eigenvector matrix. The basis-existence statement
below is a theorem; no general Jordan algorithm is required for the example.
:::

---

### A chain supplies the missing second direction {#a-chain-supplies-the-missing-second-direction}

Return to the matrix with only one independent eigenvector:

$$
\mat{J}=\begin{bmatrix}2&1\\0&2\end{bmatrix},\qquad
\vct{v}=\begin{bmatrix}1\\0\end{bmatrix},\quad
\vct{w}=\begin{bmatrix}0\\1\end{bmatrix}
$$

$$
(\mat{J}-2\mat{I})\vct{v}=\vct{0},\qquad
(\mat{J}-2\mat{I})\vct{w}=\vct{v},\qquad
(\mat{J}-2\mat{I})^2\vct{w}=\vct{0}
$$

The two vectors form a basis $\mat{G}=[\vct{v}\ \vct{w}]$, with

$$
\mat{J}\mat{G}
=\mat{G}\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}2&1\\0&2\end{bmatrix}}_{\text{Jordan block}}
$$

::: {.key-point}
The missing eigenvector is replaced by a generalized eigenvector

The off-diagonal $1$ records the coupling; the matrix is still not diagonalizable
:::

::: {.notes}
Here G=I because J is already a Jordan block. The basis still illustrates
the distinction: its second column is generalized, not an ordinary
eigenvector. A vector av+bw is sent to (2a+b)v+2bw. Thus the diagonal
entries scale coefficients while the off-diagonal entry mixes them.
The nonzero off-diagonal entry cannot be removed by choosing a different
ordinary eigenvector basis, because the eigenspace has dimension one.
:::

---

### Generalized eigenspaces supply a full basis {#generalized-eigenspaces-supply-a-full-basis}

For $\mat{A}\in\reals^{n\times n}$, suppose all characteristic roots are real, with distinct roots
$\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_s$ and algebraic multiplicities $k_1,\ldots,k_s$

$$
G_{\lambda_j}=\nullspace\bigl((\mat{A}-\lambda_j\mat{I}_n)^{k_j}\bigr),
\qquad\dim G_{\lambda_j}=k_j,\qquad\sum_{j=1}^s k_j=n
$$

Choose a basis of each $G_{\lambda_j}$ and combine the lists

The result is $n$ independent generalized eigenvectors $\vct{g}_1,\ldots,\vct{g}_n$:

$$
\boxed{\operatorname{span}\{\vct{g}_1,\ldots,\vct{g}_n\}=\reals^n}
$$

::: {.key-point}
A generalized eigenvector basis gives coordinates even when an ordinary eigenvector basis is missing

With nonreal roots, work over $\mathbb{C}$ instead: the span is $\mathbb{C}^n$
:::

::: {.notes}
State the generalized-eigenspace decomposition as a theorem. When the
characteristic polynomial splits over the scalar field, each generalized
eigenspace has dimension equal to the corresponding algebraic multiplicity,
and the generalized eigenspaces for distinct eigenvalues form a direct sum
of the whole space. Hence their individual bases combine into a basis.
Over C splitting always holds; over R the displayed real conclusion needs
all roots real. An arbitrary independent subset does not necessarily span:
we need n independent vectors in dimension n. Generalized eigenvectors
include ordinary eigenvectors, so a complete list can contain both kinds.
If the root has multiplicity one, its generalized eigenspace equals its
ordinary eigenspace. A scalar matrix can have a repeated root with no new
directions in higher kernels: its ordinary eigenspace already fills the
corresponding generalized eigenspace. Thus a repeated root does not require
a genuinely higher-order vector.
For the preceding J, k=2, G_2=null((J-2I)^2)=R^2 and {v,w} is such a basis.
For the earlier diag(J,3) example F, G_2=span{e1,e2} and G_3=span{e3}.
Do not claim an arbitrary generalized basis gives canonical Jordan blocks;
chain-adapted choices give that additional form. Coupling may remain, so this
theorem does not assert diagonalizability or the ordinary eigenmode formula.

Sources: [University of Lethbridge: generalized eigenvectors](https://opentext.uleth.ca/Math3410/sec-gen-eigen.html)
and [Treil: advanced spectral theory](https://www.math.brown.edu/streil/papers/LADW/HTML_2026_08-31/Ch9.html).
:::

## Similarity changes coordinates, not the operator {#similarity-changes-coordinates-not-the-operator}

Matrices $\mat{A}$ and $\mat{B}$ are [similar]{.alert} when

$$
\mat{B}=\mat{P}^{-1}\mat{A}\mat{P},\qquad\mat{P}\text{ invertible}
$$

Their characteristic polynomials agree:

$$
\det(\lambda\mat{I}-\mat{B})
=\det\bigl(\mat{P}^{-1}(\lambda\mat{I}-\mat{A})\mat{P}\bigr)
=\det(\lambda\mat{I}-\mat{A})
$$

- Same eigenvalues, multiplicities, trace, and determinant
- If $\mat{B}\vct{c}=\lambda\vct{c}$, then $\mat{A}(\mat{P}\vct{c})=\lambda\mat{P}\vct{c}$
- Eigenvector coordinate columns usually change

::: {.key-point}
Diagonalization is similarity to a diagonal matrix; ordinary row reduction is a different operation
:::

::: {.notes}
The identity lambda I=P^{-1}(lambda I)P gives the displayed factorization.
The nonzero determinant factors of P cancel. Similarity also preserves
rank and eigenspace dimensions, via the invertible coordinate change.
Row operations are left multiplication by an invertible matrix; similarity
requires matching inverse changes on the left and right. For example
rref(diag(2,3))=I changes its eigenvalues. Equal characteristic polynomials
alone do not imply similarity: S and J in the repeated-root example differ
in eigenspace dimension. Avoid treating eigenvalues as a full classification.
:::

# Complex Eigenvalues {#complex-eigenvalues}

A real matrix may need complex coordinates to reveal its eigenvectors

- [A quarter turn has no real eigendirection](#a-quarter-turn-has-no-real-eigendirection)
- [Complex coordinates reveal two eigenvectors](#complex-coordinates-reveal-two-eigenvectors)
- [Real matrices pair their nonreal eigenvalues](#real-matrices-pair-their-nonreal-eigenvalues)
- [Practice interpreting a rotation and scaling](#practice-interpreting-a-rotation-and-scaling)

## A quarter turn has no real eigendirection {#a-quarter-turn-has-no-real-eigendirection}

$$
\mat{R}=\begin{bmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{bmatrix},\qquad
\mat{R}\begin{bmatrix}x\\y\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-y\\x\end{bmatrix}
$$

Every nonzero real vector turns through $90^\circ$; none stays on its line

$$
p_{\mat{R}}(\lambda)=\lambda^2+1
$$

- Over $\reals$: no roots, no eigenvectors, no diagonalization
- Over $\mathbb{C}$: roots $i,-i$, where $i^2=-1$

::: {.key-point}
Always name the scalar field when deciding whether an eigenvector basis exists
:::

::: {.notes}
R maps real vectors to real vectors and has determinant 1; absence of real
eigenvectors does not imply singularity. A 180-degree rotation is different:
-I has every nonzero real vector as an eigenvector. On C^2 the same matrix
acts complex-linearly, with two distinct eigenvalues. This is an extension
of the scalar field, as in the oscillator example in Bases and Coordinates.
:::

## Complex coordinates reveal two eigenvectors {#complex-coordinates-reveal-two-eigenvectors}

For the quarter-turn matrix, direct multiplication gives

$$
\mat{R}\begin{bmatrix}1\\-i\end{bmatrix}
=\begin{bmatrix}i\\1\end{bmatrix}
=i\begin{bmatrix}1\\-i\end{bmatrix},\qquad
\mat{R}\begin{bmatrix}1\\i\end{bmatrix}
=\begin{bmatrix}-i\\1\end{bmatrix}
=-i\begin{bmatrix}1\\i\end{bmatrix}
$$

Thus, over $\mathbb{C}$,

$$
\mat{V}=\begin{bmatrix}1&1\\-i&i\end{bmatrix},\qquad
\mat{D}=\begin{bmatrix}i&0\\0&-i\end{bmatrix},\qquad
\mat{R}=\mat{V}\mat{D}\mat{V}^{-1}
$$

For real $x,y$:

$$
\begin{bmatrix}x\\y\end{bmatrix}
=\frac{x+iy}{2}\begin{bmatrix}1\\-i\end{bmatrix}
+\frac{x-iy}{2}\begin{bmatrix}1\\i\end{bmatrix}
$$

::: {.key-point}
Conjugate coefficients and eigenvectors reconstruct a real vector
:::

::: {.notes}
The determinant of V is 2i, so V is invertible. Its inverse is
(1/2)[[1,i],[1,-i]]. The coordinate formula follows by multiplication.
Applying R multiplies the first coefficient by i and the second by -i;
they remain conjugates, and their reconstruction is real. Do not draw the
complex eigenvectors as real planar arrows. The actual real motion is
still a quarter turn, not two real stretches.
:::

## Real matrices pair their nonreal eigenvalues {#real-matrices-pair-their-nonreal-eigenvalues}

If $\mat{A}$ has real entries and $\mat{A}\vct{v}=\lambda\vct{v}$, conjugate both sides:

$$
\mat{A}\overline{\vct{v}}=\overline{\lambda}\,\overline{\vct{v}}
$$

Nonreal eigenvalues and their eigenvectors occur in conjugate pairs

For $\lambda=a+ib$, $\vct{v}=\vct{p}+i\vct{q}$, equate real and imaginary parts:

$$
\mat{A}\vct{p}=a\vct{p}-b\vct{q},\qquad
\mat{A}\vct{q}=b\vct{p}+a\vct{q}
$$

When $b\ne0$, $\vct{p},\vct{q}$ span a real invariant plane

::: {.key-point}
A complex pair describes a real two-dimensional action, even without real eigenvectors in that plane
:::

::: {.notes}
For b nonzero, p and q are real-linearly independent. Otherwise v would
be a nonzero complex scalar times a real vector w, giving A w=lambda w,
impossible for a nonreal lambda and real nonzero w. In the ordered real
basis {p,q}, the plane action has matrix [[a,b],[-b,a]]. This is rotation
and uniform scaling in those coordinates, but p and q need not be
orthonormal, so it need not be Euclidean rotation/scaling in the original
coordinates. The next exercise uses a matrix already expressed in an
orthonormal standard basis, where the geometric interpretation is literal.
:::

## Practice interpreting a rotation and scaling {#practice-interpreting-a-rotation-and-scaling}

$$
\mat{B}=\begin{bmatrix}1&-1\\1&1\end{bmatrix}
$$

::: {.exitem .lettered}
<span class="exbullet">$\exstar$</span>
<span>Compare real geometry with complex coordinates
<span class="exsub">Find the characteristic polynomial, eigenvalues, and an eigenvector for each</span>
<span class="exsub">Is $\mat{B}$ diagonalizable over $\reals$? Over $\mathbb{C}$?</span>
<span class="exsub">Compute $\mat{B}\vct{e}_1$ and $\mat{B}\vct{e}_2$; identify the rotation angle and length factor</span>
</span>
:::

::: {.notes}
p_B=(lambda-1)^2+1, roots 1+i,1-i, with eigenvectors [1,-i]^T
and [1,i]^T respectively. Not diagonalizable over R; diagonalizable over
C because there are two distinct complex eigenvalues. B e1=[1,1]^T,
B e2=[-1,1]^T. Both axes rotate counterclockwise 45 degrees and scale
by sqrt(2); B=sqrt(2) R_(pi/4). B^T B=2I verifies the length factor
for every real vector, not just the axes.
:::
