## Leontief review: demand determines production {#leontief-production-adds-successive-rounds-of-inputs}

[Two-sector model from {{< meta decks.d02.short_title >}}]({{< meta decks.d02.file >}}#production-creates-internal-demand): same input matrix, a new demand forecast

$$
\mat{C}=\begin{bmatrix}0.20&0.10\\0.30&0.25\end{bmatrix},\qquad
\vct{d}=\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}74\\15\end{bmatrix}}_{\text{external demand by sector}}
$$

$c_{ij}$ — sector $i$ input needed per unit of sector $j$ output

Entry $i$ refers to sector $i$ in each vector

\begin{align*}
\underbrace{\vct{x}}_{\text{total production by sector}}
&=\underbrace{\mat{C}\vct{x}}_{\text{internal demand}}
+\underbrace{\vct{d}}_{\text{external demand}}\\
(\mat{I}-\mat{C})\vct{x}
&=\begin{bmatrix}0.80&-0.10\\-0.30&0.75\end{bmatrix}\vct{x}
=\begin{bmatrix}74\\15\end{bmatrix}
\end{align*}

::: {.key-point}
Find production first by elimination, then explain it using an eigenvector basis
:::

::: {.notes}
The input-requirements matrix is unchanged from Deck 02. That deck used
external demand [72,30]^T and production [100,80]^T. This new forecast is
chosen so both eigenbasis demand coordinates and production coordinates are
whole numbers. All quantities use consistent sector-output units. Cx gives
intermediate inputs; (I-C)x gives the external demand a production plan can
meet. This is a static balance model. Successive input rounds below are
layers of requirements, not observations at successive times.
:::

---

### Row echelon form recovers gross production {#leontief-row-echelon-solve}

Scale the first equation by $10$ and the second by $20$

$$
\left[\begin{array}{rr|r}8&-1&740\\-6&15&300\end{array}\right]
\xrightarrow{\substack{R_2\leftarrow4R_2\\R_2\leftarrow R_2+3R_1}}
\left[\begin{array}{rr|r}8&-1&740\\0&57&3420\end{array}\right]
$$

Back substitution gives

\begin{align*}
57x_2=3420&\implies x_2=60\\
8x_1-x_2=740&\implies x_1=100
\end{align*}

Two [pivots]({{< meta decks.d01.file >}}#pivots-organize-elimination) — one unique production plan

$$
\vct{x}=\begin{bmatrix}100\\60\end{bmatrix},\qquad
\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}26\\45\end{bmatrix}}_{\mat{C}\vct{x}}
+\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}74\\15\end{bmatrix}}_{\vct{d}}
=\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}100\\60\end{bmatrix}}_{\vct{x}}
$$

::: {.notes}
The two arrow labels are successive elementary row operations: multiply
row 2 by 4, then add 3 times row 1. The scaled system has the same solution
as the original. Echelon form and back substitution suffice; no RREF or
explicit inverse is needed. Both coefficient columns have pivots, so the
square system has a unique solution for every demand. The final check
also verifies the economic balance and nonnegative production.
:::

---

### Find the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of the input matrix {#leontief-eigenpairs}

Scaling preserves the eigendirections; use a trial vector $\vct{v}=[a,b]^\top$

$$
\mat{M}=20\mat{C}=\begin{bmatrix}4&2\\6&5\end{bmatrix}
$$

$$
p_{\mat{M}}(\mu)=\det(\mu\mat{I}-\mat{M})
=(\mu-4)(\mu-5)-12=(\mu-8)(\mu-1)
$$

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="47%"}
$\mu_1=8$: $-4a+2b=0$

$$
\vct{v}_1=\begin{bmatrix}1\\2\end{bmatrix},\qquad
\mat{C}\vct{v}_1=\frac25\vct{v}_1
$$
:::
::: {.column width="6%"}
:::
::: {.column width="47%"}
$\mu_2=1$: $3a+2b=0$

$$
\vct{v}_2=\begin{bmatrix}2\\-3\end{bmatrix},\qquad
\mat{C}\vct{v}_2=\frac1{20}\vct{v}_2
$$
:::
:::

::: {.key-point}
The eigenvalues of $\mat{C}$ are $2/5=0.4$ and $1/20=0.05$
:::

::: {.notes}
Use scalar entries a,b in the trial vector; bold v_j names one of the two
complete eigenvectors. An eigenvalue mu of M=20C corresponds to lambda=mu/20
of C. The monic characteristic polynomial follows Anton. Each displayed
linear equation comes from (M-mu I)v=0; the second row is dependent.
Directly check Cv1=[0.4,0.8]^T and Cv2=[0.1,-0.15]^T. Distinct eigenvalues
make these two eigenvectors independent, hence a basis of R^2.
:::

---

### Subtracting from the identity preserves the eigenvectors {#leontief-shared-eigenvectors}

For each eigenpair of $\mat{C}$,

$$
\mat{C}\vct{v}_j=\lambda_j\vct{v}_j
\implies
(\mat{I}-\mat{C})\vct{v}_j=(1-\lambda_j)\vct{v}_j
$$

Multipliers along each eigendirection

| Direction | Internal requirements<br>$\mat{C}$: $\lambda_j$ | Net output<br>$\mat{I}-\mat{C}$: $1-\lambda_j$ | Total output<br>$\mat{I}$: $1$ |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| $\vct{v}_1=[1,2]^\top$ | $2/5$ | $3/5$ | $1$ |
| $\vct{v}_2=[2,-3]^\top$ | $1/20$ | $19/20$ | $1$ |

Both net-output multipliers are nonzero — $\mat{I}-\mat{C}$ is invertible

::: {.key-point}
The same eigendirections describe total output, internal requirements and net output
:::

::: {.notes}
The displayed implication works for every eigenvector without assuming
diagonalizability. Here the two vectors form a basis, so the two nonzero
multipliers prove invertibility. Conversely, if (I-C)v=eta v, then
Cv=(1-eta)v; the eigenspaces are exactly the same, with shifted eigenvalues.
The second line of each table header identifies the matrix and its scalar
multiplier on v_j. Total output is the identity action, with multiplier 1;
internal requirements use lambda_j and net output uses 1-lambda_j.
Invertibility needs lambda not equal to 1. The stronger magnitude-below-1
condition will justify the geometric series and iteration later.
:::

---

### Interpret a production mix and a sector adjustment {#leontief-interpret-eigendirections}

For total output in an eigendirection,

$$
\mat{C}\vct{x}=\lambda\vct{x},\qquad
\vct{d}=\vct{x}-\mat{C}\vct{x}=(1-\lambda)\vct{x}
$$

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="47%"}
$\vct{v}_1=[1,2]^\top$ — a feasible production mix in the ratio $1:2$

- Internal inputs keep the same mix: $\mat{C}\vct{v}_1=0.4\vct{v}_1$
- Net output for external demand: $0.6\vct{v}_1$
- Demand in this direction needs $5/3$ times as much gross production
:::
::: {.column width="6%"}
:::
::: {.column width="47%"}
$\vct{v}_2=[2,-3]^\top$ — increase sector 1, decrease sector 2

- Internal-input change: $0.05\vct{v}_2$
- External-demand change: $0.95\vct{v}_2$
- A negative entry means a decrease from an existing production level
:::
:::

::: {.key-point}
Internal demand, external demand and total output are parallel in an eigendirection
:::

::: {.notes}
A nonnegative multiple of v1 is a feasible gross-production profile; its
internal requirements and net output have the same sector ratio. v2 has
opposite signs, so it is not a feasible production plan by itself. By
linearity it describes a small signed change around a baseline with enough
production in both sectors: delta x=a v2 implies delta d=0.95a v2.
This interprets a right eigenvector of C, not a left price eigenvector.
Neither individual eigendirection represents the complete new forecast;
both components contribute to d and x.
The external output is the net output x-Cx that satisfies external demand d.
Thus x, Cx and d are scalar multiples of one another along an eigendirection;
for the signed second mode, interpret the relation as parallel changes in
these three quantities. Both eigenvalues here lie strictly between 0 and 1,
so neither internal demand nor net output vanishes along a nonzero mode.
:::

---

### A basis turns the demand vector into coordinates {#leontief-basis-and-coordinates}

Use the ordered eigenbasis $\mathcal{V}=\{\vct{v}_1,\vct{v}_2\}$

$$
\mat{V}=[\vct{v}_1\ \vct{v}_2]
=\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\2&-3\end{bmatrix},\qquad
\mat{V}^{-1}=\frac17\begin{bmatrix}3&2\\2&-1\end{bmatrix}
$$

Read the coordinates, then reconstruct the same demand

\begin{align*}
[\vct{d}]_{\mathcal{V}}
&=\mat{V}^{-1}\begin{bmatrix}74\\15\end{bmatrix}
=\begin{bmatrix}36\\19\end{bmatrix}\\
\vct{d}&=36\vct{v}_1+19\vct{v}_2
=[\vct{v}_1\ \vct{v}_2]\begin{bmatrix}36\\19\end{bmatrix}
=\begin{bmatrix}74\\15\end{bmatrix}
\end{align*}

::: {.key-point}
The entries $36,19$ describe demand in the eigenbasis; $74,15$ describe sector demand
:::

::: {.notes}
The basis is a set listed in a specified order; coordinate entry j multiplies
v_j, and V uses that same column order. det(V)=-7, so the representation is
unique. V maps eigenbasis coordinate columns to standard sector vectors;
V^-1 reads eigenbasis coordinates. These eigenvectors are not perpendicular:
v1^T v2=-4, which reinforces that a basis need not be orthogonal. The numbers
36 and 19 are coordinates, not the individual sectors' external demands.
:::

---

### Solve the same system in eigenbasis coordinates {#leontief-solve-in-eigenbasis}

Let $\vct{c}=[\vct{x}]_{\mathcal{V}}$ and $\mat{D}=\operatorname{diag}(2/5,1/20)$

$$
\mat{C}=\mat{V}\mat{D}\mat{V}^{-1},\qquad
(\mat{I}-\mat{C})\mat{V}\vct{c}=\vct{d}
$$

Change coordinates to separate the two equations

$$
\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}3/5&0\\0&19/20\end{bmatrix}}_{\mat{I}-\mat{D}}
\begin{bmatrix}c_1\\c_2\end{bmatrix}
=\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}36\\19\end{bmatrix}}_{[\vct{d}]_{\mathcal{V}}}
\implies \vct{c}=\begin{bmatrix}60\\20\end{bmatrix}
$$

$$
\vct{x}=\mat{V}\vct{c}
=60\vct{v}_1+20\vct{v}_2
=\begin{bmatrix}100\\60\end{bmatrix}
$$

::: {.key-point}
Read demand coordinates, divide by $1-\lambda_j$, then reconstruct production
:::

::: {.notes}
Multiplying the standard-coordinate system by V^-1 gives (I-D)c=V^-1d.
Thus c1=36/(3/5)=60 and c2=19/(19/20)=20. This reproduces the elimination
answer. The complete map is x=V(I-D)^-1 V^-1 d. Eigenvectors describe whole
production directions; c is the coordinate column of the unknown vector.
Diagonalizing is a conceptual/reusable description, not a claim that it is
the fastest way to solve every numerical system.
:::

---

### Decompose production into a mix and an adjustment {#leontief-production-decomposition}

The production coordinates $[\vct{x}]_{\mathcal{V}}=[60,20]^\top$ give

\begin{align*}
\vct{x}&=60\vct{v}_1+20\vct{v}_2\\
&=\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}60\\120\end{bmatrix}}_{\text{baseline production}}
+\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}40\\-60\end{bmatrix}}_{\text{signed adjustment}}
=\begin{bmatrix}100\\60\end{bmatrix}
\end{align*}

Increase sector 1 by $40$; decrease sector 2 by $60$ — both final outputs remain nonnegative

| Quantity | Baseline | Adjustment | Result |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Internal demand $\mat{C}\vct{x}$ | $[24,48]^\top$ | $[2,-3]^\top$ | $[26,45]^\top$ |
| External demand $\vct{d}$ | $[36,72]^\top$ | $[38,-57]^\top$ | $[74,15]^\top$ |

::: {.key-point}
One eigenvector describes a production mix; the other describes a sector adjustment
:::

::: {.notes}
Place this worked economic interpretation after the eigenbasis solve so the
coordinates 60 and 20 have already been derived. The baseline 60v1 is a
feasible production plan with its own nonnegative external demand [36,72]^T.
The adjustment 20v2 raises sector 1 by 40 and lowers sector 2 by 60, yielding
the new feasible plan [100,60]^T. A negative adjustment entry represents a
decrease from the baseline, not a negative final production level.
By linearity, C(20v2)=0.05(20v2)=[2,-3]^T and
(I-C)(20v2)=0.95(20v2)=[38,-57]^T. Adding these to the baseline's
internal requirements [24,48]^T and external demand [36,72]^T gives the
original checked totals. The table therefore applies the same decomposition
to total production, internal demand and external demand; the table's
entries are sector vectors, not eigenvalues. These are static comparisons
between production plans, not a time-dependent adjustment model.
:::

---

### Powers add successive rounds of input requirements {#leontief-input-rounds}

External demand $\vct{d}$ needs inputs $\mat{C}\vct{d}$, which need $\mat{C}^2\vct{d}$, and so on

Since $\vct{d}=36\vct{v}_1+19\vct{v}_2$,

$$
\mat{C}^k\vct{d}
=36\left(\frac25\right)^k\vct{v}_1
+19\left(\frac1{20}\right)^k\vct{v}_2,\qquad k\ge0
$$

Both eigenvalues have magnitude below $1$ — the input-round vectors tend to zero

\begin{align*}
\vct{x}
&=\vct{d}+\mat{C}\vct{d}+\mat{C}^2\vct{d}+\cdots\\
&=\frac{36}{1-2/5}\vct{v}_1+\frac{19}{1-1/20}\vct{v}_2\\
&=60\vct{v}_1+20\vct{v}_2=\begin{bmatrix}100\\60\end{bmatrix}
\end{align*}

::: {.notes}
Each round is another layer of intermediate inputs in the static model.
Apply C repeatedly to each eigenvector to obtain the scalar powers; at k=0
both scalar powers equal 1. The mixed demand does not shrink by one common
factor each round. The earlier special demand [3,6]^T was 3v1 and therefore
had only the 0.4 mode; retain that as an optional spoken simplification.
Here Cd=[16.3,25.95]^T: sector 2's first input requirement exceeds its
external demand 15. Convergence to zero does not mean every sector decreases
at every round. The identity x-Cx=[74,15]^T checks the sum. The general
powers formula follows immediately after this worked review.
:::

---

### A matrix geometric series gives an iterative solve {#leontief-matrix-series-and-iteration}

For this model, every eigenvalue of $\mat{C}$ has magnitude below $1$

$$
(\mat{I}-\mat{C})^{-1}=\mat{I}+\mat{C}+\mat{C}^2+\cdots
$$

Start with $\vct{x}^{(0)}=\vct{0}$ and add one layer of inputs per step

\begin{align*}
\vct{x}^{(k+1)}&=\mat{C}\vct{x}^{(k)}+\vct{d}\\
\vct{x}^{(1)}&=\vct{d},\qquad
\vct{x}^{(2)}=\vct{d}+\mat{C}\vct{d}\\
\vct{x}^{(k)}&=\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}\mat{C}^j\vct{d}
\longrightarrow(\mat{I}-\mat{C})^{-1}\vct{d}
\end{align*}

::: {.key-point}
Repeated matrix–vector products approach the same production plan without forming an inverse
:::

::: {.notes}
This preserves the earlier iterative-solve addition. It is fixed-point
iteration for x=Cx+d, equivalently a stationary iterative method for (I-C)x=d.
For any initial guess, e^(k+1)=C e^(k), where e^(k)=x-x^(k), so e^(k)=C^k e^(0).
The finite identity (I-C)(I+C+...+C^m)=I-C^(m+1) proves the inverse formula
when C^k tends to zero. For any square matrix, eigenvalues of magnitude below
1 suffice; diagonalizability is not required. Invertibility alone does not
guarantee convergence of this particular iteration. For a sparse C with s
nonzero entries, a step costs O(s+n) and stores C, d and the current iterate.
This may help large sparse systems but is not always better than a direct
solve. Eigenvalues near the unit circle give slow asymptotic convergence;
a nonnormal matrix can also show transient error growth.
:::

---

### The production response is a matrix function {#leontief-response-matrix-function}

The scalar response $f(z)=1/(1-z)$ acts on each eigendirection

$$
f(\mat{C})=(\mat{I}-\mat{C})^{-1}
=\mat{V}\begin{bmatrix}5/3&0\\0&20/19\end{bmatrix}\mat{V}^{-1},\qquad
\vct{x}=f(\mat{C})\vct{d}
$$

| Action in the same eigenbasis | Scalar multiplier on $\vct{v}_j$ |
|---|---:|
| Internal inputs $\mat{C}$ | $\lambda_j$ |
| Net output $\mat{I}-\mat{C}$ | $1-\lambda_j$ |
| Input round $\mat{C}^k$ | $\lambda_j^k$ |
| Production response $(\mat{I}-\mat{C})^{-1}$ | $1/(1-\lambda_j)$ |

::: {.key-point}
One eigenvector basis connects linear systems, coordinates, powers and matrix functions
:::

::: {.notes}
The response is the matrix function f(C), not entrywise application of
1/(1-z) to the four entries of C. The basis vectors are unchanged while
the scalar multipliers change. The rational response only needs 1 not to
be an eigenvalue; representing it by the displayed geometric series also
needs all eigenvalues to have magnitude below 1. The general powers and
matrix-function formulas now summarize what this practical example earned.
:::

## Powers act separately on eigenbasis coordinates {#powers-act-separately-on-eigenbasis-coordinates}

If $\mat{A}=\mat{V}\mat{D}\mat{V}^{-1}$, cancellation gives, for integers $k\ge0$,

$$
\mat{A}^k=\mat{V}\mat{D}^k\mat{V}^{-1},\qquad
\mat{D}^k=\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1^k,\ldots,\lambda_n^k)
$$

If $\vct{x}_0=\sum_{j=1}^n c_j\vct{v}_j$, then

$$
\vct{x}_k=\mat{A}^k\vct{x}_0
=\sum_{j=1}^n c_j\lambda_j^k\vct{v}_j
$$

- $|\lambda_j|<1$: that component tends to zero
- $\lambda_j=1$: that component stays fixed
- $\lambda_j=-1$: that component alternates sign
- $|\lambda_j|>1$: a nonzero component grows in magnitude

::: {.notes}
A^0=I and D^0=I by definition, including when an eigenvalue is zero; avoid
interpreting the k=0 case as a scalar 0^0 limit. For k>=1 the powers are
ordinary scalar powers. Negative powers require A invertible. Complex
components include phase changes; their magnitudes scale by |lambda|^k.
This formula assumes an eigenvector basis. A missing initial component
c_j=0 stays absent, so a large eigenvalue does not make every initial vector
grow. The optional generalized-eigenvector topic introduces a coupled Jordan
block; powers of defective matrices and a general Jordan algorithm are not
developed here.
:::

## Functions act separately on eigenbasis coordinates {#functions-act-separately-on-eigenbasis-coordinates}

If $\mat{A}=\mat{V}\mat{D}\mat{V}^{-1}$ and $f$ is defined at every eigenvalue, define

\begin{equation*}
f(\mat{A})=\mat{V}\,\operatorname{diag}\bigl(f(\lambda_1),\ldots,f(\lambda_n)\bigr)\,\mat{V}^{-1}
\end{equation*}

Each eigenvector is scaled by the corresponding scalar value:

\begin{equation*}
f(\mat{A})\vct{v}_j=f(\lambda_j)\vct{v}_j
\end{equation*}

| Scalar function | Matrix function |
|---|---|
| $f(z)=z^k$, integer $k\ge0$ | $\mat{A}^k$ |
| $f(z)=1/z$, no zero eigenvalue | $\mat{A}^{-1}$ |
| $f(z)=1/(1-z)$, no eigenvalue $1$ | $(\mat{I}-\mat{A})^{-1}$ |
| $f(z)=e^{tz}$ | $e^{t\mat{A}}$ |

::: {.key-point}
Apply $f$ to the eigenvalues, then change back — not to the individual matrix entries
:::

::: {.notes}
This definition assumes a complete eigenvector basis over the chosen scalar
field, and f must be defined at all eigenvalues. It is independent of the
eigenvector ordering, scaling and choice of basis within a repeated eigenspace.
For a polynomial p, cancellation in powers gives the usual p(A). A convergent
power series similarly agrees with this formula. Do not claim this prescription
defines arbitrary matrix functions for defective matrices; the exponential on
the next slide is defined for all square matrices by its convergent series.
For k=0, use the constant function f(z)=1, including at zero.
The companion checks p(A)=A^2-2A for the running example.
:::

---

### Taylor series give more matrix functions {#taylor-series-give-more-matrix-functions}

For $\mat{A}=\mat{V}\mat{D}\mat{V}^{-1}$, let the [Taylor series]{.alert}
$f(z)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}a_kz^k$ converge at every eigenvalue

\begin{equation*}
f(\mat{A})=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}a_k\mat{A}^k
=\mat{V}\operatorname{diag}\bigl(f(\lambda_1),\ldots,f(\lambda_n)\bigr)\mat{V}^{-1}
\end{equation*}

For example,

\begin{align*}
\sin(\mat{A})&=\mat{A}-\frac{\mat{A}^3}{3!}+\frac{\mat{A}^5}{5!}-\cdots\\
\cos(\mat{A})&=\mat{I}-\frac{\mat{A}^2}{2!}+\frac{\mat{A}^4}{4!}-\cdots
\end{align*}

::: {.key-point}
The same series coefficients; matrix powers replace scalar powers
:::

::: {.notes}
For a diagonalizable matrix, convergence at every eigenvalue gives convergence
of the matrix series. For a Taylor series centered at a, replace scalar powers
(z-a)^k by (A-aI)^k. The sine and cosine series converge for every square
matrix, even without diagonalizability. These are matrix series, not
entrywise sine and cosine. The exponential is the next example.
:::

## The matrix exponential solves a linear differential system {#the-matrix-exponential-solves-a-linear-differential-system}

For any square matrix, define the [matrix exponential]{.alert}

\begin{equation*}
e^{t\mat{A}}=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{t^k\mat{A}^k}{k!}
=\mat{I}+t\mat{A}+\frac{t^2}{2}\mat{A}^2+\cdots
\end{equation*}

For a constant matrix, the [linear differential system]({{< meta decks.d06.file >}}#homogeneous-linear-des-give-vector-spaces)
has the unique solution

\begin{equation*}
\vct{x}'=\mat{A}\vct{x},\quad\vct{x}(0)=\vct{x}_0
\qquad\implies\qquad
\vct{x}(t)=e^{t\mat{A}}\vct{x}_0
\end{equation*}

If $\mat{A}$ has an [eigenvector basis]{.alert},

\begin{equation*}
e^{t\mat{A}}=\mat{V}e^{t\mat{D}}\mat{V}^{-1},\qquad
e^{t\mat{D}}=\operatorname{diag}(e^{t\lambda_1},\ldots,e^{t\lambda_n})
\end{equation*}

::: {.key-point}
The matrix exponential works for every square matrix; the diagonal formula needs an eigenbasis
:::

::: {.notes}
A is constant and t is real. The series converges for every finite square A
and every finite t. Termwise differentiation gives E'(t)=A E(t) and E(0)=I,
so E(t)x0 solves the initial-value problem, even if A is not diagonalizable.
Uniqueness follows, for example, by differentiating e^(-tA)x(t): the product
is constant and equals x0. The derivative identity uses that A commutes
with its exponential. Only the eigenbasis formulas require diagonalizability.
Real parts of eigenvalues determine
exponential growth/decay for complex modes; no general stability theory is
required here. The identity at t=0 is I, not a matrix of entrywise exponentials.
Unlike A itself, e^(tA) is always invertible, with inverse e^(-tA).
A zero eigenvalue gives a constant ODE mode, not a collapsed solution:
e^(t*0)=1. In discrete steps lambda=1 is fixed; in continuous time lambda=0
is an equilibrium direction. Avoid interchanging multipliers and rates.
:::

---

### Eigenbasis coordinates decouple a differential system {#eigenbasis-coordinates-decouple-a-differential-system}

Let $\mat{A}=\mat{V}\mat{D}\mat{V}^{-1}$ and write
$\vct{x}(t)=\mat{V}\vct{c}(t)$

The basis matrix is constant, so

\begin{equation*}
\vct{x}'=\mat{A}\vct{x}
\iff\mat{V}\vct{c}'=\mat{A}\mat{V}\vct{c}=\mat{V}\mat{D}\vct{c}
\iff\boxed{\vct{c}'=\mat{D}\vct{c}}
\end{equation*}

Each coordinate solves its own scalar equation:

\begin{equation*}
c_j'(t)=\lambda_jc_j(t)
\quad\implies\quad
c_j(t)=e^{\lambda_jt}c_j(0)
\end{equation*}

\begin{equation*}
\boxed{\vct{x}(t)=\mat{V}e^{t\mat{D}}\mat{V}^{-1}\vct{x}_0}
\end{equation*}

\begin{equation*}
\vct{x}(t)
\xleftarrow{\ \mat{V}\ }
\vct{c}(t)
\xleftarrow{\ e^{t\mat{D}}\ }
\underbrace{\vct{c}_0}_{\text{initial coordinates}}
\xleftarrow{\ \mat{V}^{-1}\ }
\underbrace{\vct{x}_0}_{\text{initial state}}
\end{equation*}

::: {.key-point}
Read right to left: change to the eigenbasis, evolve each coordinate, then reconstruct
:::

::: {.notes}
Both the state and its velocity use the same constant basis. A time-dependent
basis would contribute a V'(t)c(t) term and is not under discussion here.
Define c0=c(0)=V^{-1}x0. The evolving c_j(t) is not a constant; its initial
value c_j(0) is the fixed coefficient of the solution mode. For a complex
eigenbasis of a real matrix, conjugate modes reconstruct real solutions.
Read both the boxed product and the arrow line from right to left:
V^{-1}x0 gives the initial
eigenbasis coordinates, e^(tD) evolves them, and V reconstructs the current
state. The factor x0 is essential for a solution vector. Without x0,
V e^(tD) V^{-1}=e^(tA) is the evolution matrix, not the state vector.
:::

---

### Example: two exponential modes {#example-two-exponential-modes}

Return to $\mat{A}=\begin{bmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{bmatrix}$ and $\vct{x}(0)=\begin{bmatrix}1\\0\end{bmatrix}$

The eigenvectors $\vct{v}_1=[1,1]^\top$, $\vct{v}_2=[1,-1]^\top$ have eigenvalues $3,1$

\begin{equation*}
e^{t\mat{A}}=\frac12
\begin{bmatrix}
e^{3t}+e^t&e^{3t}-e^t\\
e^{3t}-e^t&e^{3t}+e^t
\end{bmatrix}
\end{equation*}

Since $\vct{x}(0)=(\vct{v}_1+\vct{v}_2)/2$,

\begin{equation*}
\vct{x}(t)=\frac12 e^{3t}\begin{bmatrix}1\\1\end{bmatrix}
+\frac12 e^t\begin{bmatrix}1\\-1\end{bmatrix}
=\frac12\begin{bmatrix}e^{3t}+e^t\\e^{3t}-e^t\end{bmatrix}
\end{equation*}

::: {.key-point}
Split the initial vector into eigenvectors; evolve each scalar coordinate
:::

::: {.notes}
Use V=[[1,1],[1,-1]], D=diag(3,1), V^{-1}=V/2.
At t=0 the exponential matrix is I and x(0)=[1,0]^T. Differentiating gives
x'(t)=[(3e^(3t)+e^t)/2,(3e^(3t)-e^t)/2]^T=A x(t).
The companion verifies the full matrix identity, derivative, and initial data.
Both modes grow for increasing t; the rate-3 mode dominates this initial
condition. Do not infer every solution contains that mode.
:::

---

### One trajectory in two coordinate systems {#one-trajectory-in-two-coordinate-systems}

Use the earlier initial vector $\vct{x}_0=[4,2]^\top$, so
$\vct{c}_0=\mat{V}^{-1}\vct{x}_0=[3,1]^\top$

![](assets/eigenvalues/eigenbasis-flow.svg){fig-alt="The same differential-system trajectory in original coordinates on the left and eigenbasis coordinates on the right. Read the coordinate change right to left: the initial point (3,1) in the c plane maps through V to (4,2) in the x plane. Matching dots mark the same four times; coordinate axes in the c plane correspond to diagonal eigendirections in the x plane." width="82%" .nostretch .diagram-image}

\begin{equation*}
\vct{x}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}3e^{3t}+e^t\\3e^{3t}-e^t\end{bmatrix}
\quad\xleftarrow{\quad\mat{V}\quad}\quad
\vct{c}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}3e^{3t}\\e^t\end{bmatrix}
\end{equation*}

::: {.key-point}
Same motion, different coordinates
:::

::: {.notes}
This uses the diagonalization example's x0=[4,2]^T, not the preceding
example's x0=e1. Both use the same A,V,D. Equal-time markers correspond
under V; time itself is unchanged. The plot shows states in a plane, not
individual component values plotted against time. The direction field is
velocity, so diagonal D means c1'=3c1 and c2'=c2, not straight mixed-mode
trajectories. Pure modes stay on invariant lines; a combination need not.
V is sqrt(2) times an orthogonal matrix in this particular example; a general
eigenbasis can be oblique. The plotting script verifies x=Vc and x'=Ax.
:::

## Initial data choose a whole solution {#initial-data-choose-a-whole-solution}

Use $\mathbb{K}=\reals$ or $\mathbb{K}=\mathbb{C}$; $\mathbb{K}^n$ means columns of $n$ real or complex numbers

For a constant $\mat{A}\in\mathbb{K}^{n\times n}$, let

\begin{equation*}
S_{\mat{A}}=\{\vct{x}:\reals\to\mathbb{K}^n:\vct{x}'=\mat{A}\vct{x}\}
\end{equation*}

The [solution map]{.alert} $T_{\mat{A}}:\mathbb{K}^n\to S_{\mat{A}}$ builds the whole function

::: {.eigen-map role="group" aria-label="Read right to left: the solution map T sub A maps the initial state column in the right box to the whole solution function in the left box, whose value at time t is exp(tA) times that initial state."}
<div class="diagram-node eigen-map-input">
<span class="diagram-label">Initial state in $\mathbb{K}^n$</span>
<span class="eigen-map-line">$\vct{x}_0=\begin{bmatrix}x_1(0)\\\vdots\\x_n(0)\end{bmatrix}$</span>
</div>
<div class="diagram-arrow eigen-map-arrow">$\xleftarrow{\quad T_{\mat{A}}\quad}$</div>
<div class="diagram-node eigen-map-output">
<span class="diagram-label">Whole solution in $S_{\mat{A}}$</span>
<span class="eigen-map-line">$\vct{x}(\cdot):t\longmapsto e^{t\mat{A}}\vct{x}_0$</span>
</div>
:::

Evaluation at one time: $\operatorname{ev}_t\circ T_{\mat{A}}=e^{t\mat{A}}$

::: {.key-point}
$T_{\mat{A}}$ is a linear isomorphism, with inverse $\vct{x}\mapsto\vct{x}(0)$

$\dim S_{\mat{A}}=n$, even when $\mat{A}$ is not diagonalizable
:::

::: {.notes}
S_A consists of continuously differentiable functions on all real t; the
constant-coefficient equation makes them smooth. Addition and scalar
multiplication are pointwise. Closure follows by differentiating linear
combinations. T_A is linear because e^(tA) is linear at every t. Existence
and uniqueness give a bijection: every initial vector gives exactly one
solution, and evaluating that solution at zero returns the vector.
T_A is a map into a function space, not the numerical matrix e^(tA) for one
chosen t. This generalizes the earlier initial-data-to-spring-solution map
in Bases and Coordinates. The zero vector of S_A is the zero function.
Blackboard-bold K denotes specifically R or C in this differential-equation
context; its nth power is the space of n-component columns. Choose one
scalar field consistently for both boxes.
:::

---

### An eigenbasis becomes a basis of solution functions {#an-eigenbasis-becomes-a-basis-of-solution-functions}

If $\mathcal{V}=\{\vct{v}_1,\ldots,\vct{v}_n\}$ is an eigenvector basis,
define the [solution modes]{.alert}

\begin{equation*}
\vct{\phi}_j=T_{\mat{A}}(\vct{v}_j),\qquad
\vct{\phi}_j(t)=e^{\lambda_jt}\vct{v}_j
\end{equation*}

The isomorphism carries a basis to a basis:
$\mathcal{F}=\{\vct{\phi}_1,\ldots,\vct{\phi}_n\}$ of $S_{\mat{A}}$

::: {.eigen-map role="group" aria-label="Read right to left: the solution map T sub A takes the initial vector in the right box to the whole function in the left box. Both boxes contain the same coordinate column c zero, in the eigenvector and solution-mode bases respectively."}
<div class="diagram-node eigen-map-input">
<span class="diagram-label">Initial vector</span>
<span class="eigen-map-line">$\displaystyle\vct{x}_0=\sum_{j=1}^n c_j(0)\vct{v}_j$</span>
<span class="eigen-map-line">$[\vct{x}_0]_{\mathcal{V}}=\begin{bmatrix}c_1(0)\\\vdots\\c_n(0)\end{bmatrix}$</span>
</div>
<div class="diagram-arrow eigen-map-arrow">$\xleftarrow{\quad T_{\mat{A}}\quad}$</div>
<div class="diagram-node eigen-map-output">
<span class="diagram-label">Whole solution function</span>
<span class="eigen-map-line">$\displaystyle\vct{x}(\cdot)=\sum_{j=1}^n c_j(0)\vct{\phi}_j$</span>
<span class="eigen-map-line">$[\vct{x}(\cdot)]_{\mathcal{F}}=\begin{bmatrix}c_1(0)\\\vdots\\c_n(0)\end{bmatrix}$</span>
</div>
:::

::: {.key-point}
The same coordinate column in both boxes: $[\vct{x}(\cdot)]_{\mathcal{F}}=[\vct{x}_0]_{\mathcal{V}}=\vct{c}_0$
:::

::: {.notes}
Independence can be seen without a new theorem: evaluate a zero combination
of phi_j at zero to obtain the same zero combination of v_j, forcing all
coefficients to vanish. Spanning follows by expanding any initial vector
in V and applying T_A. This remains valid for repeated eigenvalues if there
is a complete eigenbasis. The basis vectors of S_A are whole vector-valued
functions, not their values at one t. The coordinates of that whole function
are constant c_j(0); the coordinates of its current state are c_j(t).
For x0=[4,2]^T, the whole solution is 3 phi1+phi2, whereas its state at time
t has eigenbasis coordinates [3e^(3t),e^t]^T. This distinction is central.
:::

---

### Differentiation has the same eigenvalues on the solution space {#differentiation-has-the-same-eigenvalues-on-the-solution-space}

On $S_{\mat{A}}$, differentiation is a linear operator
$\mathcal{L}:\vct{x}\mapsto\vct{x}'$

Each solution mode is an [eigenfunction]{.alert} of differentiation:

\begin{equation*}
\mathcal{L}\vct{\phi}_j
=\vct{\phi}_j'
=\lambda_j\vct{\phi}_j
\end{equation*}

The solution map connects the two actions:

\begin{equation*}
\boxed{\mathcal{L}\circ T_{\mat{A}}=T_{\mat{A}}\circ\mat{A}}
\qquad
[\mathcal{L}]_{\mathcal{F}\leftarrow\mathcal{F}}=\mat{D}
\end{equation*}

::: {.key-point}
In state space: eigenvectors of a matrix

In solution space: eigenvectors are exponential solution functions
:::

::: {.notes}
This is a conceptual extension connecting abstract linear operators and
eigenvectors; it may be skipped on a first pass. Because A is constant,
if x'=Ax, then (x')'=A x', so differentiation maps S_A into itself.
For any u, (T_A u)'(t)=A e^(tA)u=e^(tA)Au=(T_A(Au))(t).
Thus L=T_A A T_A^{-1}, a similarity of operators on different spaces.
The matrix D represents A in the eigenbasis V and differentiation in the
function basis F. Applying A to initial data is distinct from advancing
time; time advancement is e^(tA). No spectrum of an infinite-dimensional
function space is needed: S_A has dimension n.
:::

---

### The earlier spring uses the same coordinate change {#the-earlier-spring-uses-the-same-coordinate-change}

Recall [$y''+y=0$ in {{< meta decks.d07.short_title >}}]({{< meta decks.d07.file >}}#initial-data-map-linearly-to-a-solution-function)
with $y(0)=a$, $y'(0)=b$

\begin{equation*}
\vct{x}=\begin{bmatrix}y\\y'\end{bmatrix}
\quad\implies\quad
\vct{x}'=\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{bmatrix}}_{\mat{H}}\vct{x},
\qquad\vct{x}_0=\begin{bmatrix}a\\b\end{bmatrix}
\end{equation*}

Over $\mathbb{C}$, choose an eigenbasis:

\begin{equation*}
\mat{V}=\begin{bmatrix}1&1\\i&-i\end{bmatrix},\qquad
\mat{D}=\begin{bmatrix}i&0\\0&-i\end{bmatrix},\qquad
\vct{c}_0=\mat{V}^{-1}\vct{x}_0
=\frac12\begin{bmatrix}a-ib\\a+ib\end{bmatrix}
\end{equation*}

The first component of $\vct{x}(t)=\mat{V}e^{t\mat{D}}\vct{c}_0$ is

\begin{equation*}
y(t)=\frac{a-ib}{2}e^{it}+\frac{a+ib}{2}e^{-it}
=a\cos(t)+b\sin(t)
\end{equation*}

::: {.key-point}
The earlier change to exponential-function coordinates comes from an eigenbasis of the first-order system
:::

::: {.notes}
H has eigenvalue i with vector [1,i]^T and eigenvalue -i with vector
[1,-i]^T. H is the negative of the earlier quarter-turn matrix R; its real
flow is clockwise in the (y,y') plane. Use the given signs, not those of R.
The inverse V^{-1}=(1/2)[[1,-i],[1,i]] is exactly the earlier transition
Q_(E<-B) from cos,sin coordinates to exp(it),exp(-it) coordinates.
For real a,b, the coefficients and vector modes are conjugate pairs; their
sum is real. The scalar spring solution and vector state solution determine
each other by y -> (y,y'), so both solution spaces have dimension two.
There is no real eigenbasis; complex coordinates are necessary for scalar
decoupling, whereas a real rotation formula still describes the motion.
For the earlier critically damped spring, the state matrix [[0,1],[-1,-2]]
has a repeated eigenvalue -1 but only one eigendirection. Its solution map
is still an isomorphism; the t exp(-t) term is a reminder that not every
solution basis consists of ordinary eigenmodes. Do not imply otherwise.
:::

---

### Real coordinates show the same oscillation {#real-coordinates-show-the-same-oscillation}

Take real initial data $a,b\in\reals$

For $\mat{H}=\begin{bmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{bmatrix}$, $\mat{H}^2=-\mat{I}$,
so the exponential series gives

\begin{equation*}
e^{t\mat{H}}=\cos(t)\mat{I}+\sin(t)\mat{H}
=\begin{bmatrix}\cos(t)&\sin(t)\\-\sin(t)&\cos(t)\end{bmatrix}
\end{equation*}

\begin{equation*}
\begin{bmatrix}y(t)\\y'(t)\end{bmatrix}
=\begin{bmatrix}a\cos(t)+b\sin(t)\\-a\sin(t)+b\cos(t)\end{bmatrix},
\qquad y(t)^2+y'(t)^2=a^2+b^2
\end{equation*}

- Real state space: clockwise circles for nonzero initial data
- Complex eigenbasis: independent factors $e^{it}$ and $e^{-it}$
- Solution space: fixed coefficients of $\cos(t),\sin(t)$ or $e^{it},e^{-it}$

::: {.key-point}
One motion connects matrix geometry, coordinates, and a basis of functions
:::

::: {.notes}
Collect even and odd powers in the exponential, using H^2=-I. The matrix
is orthogonal, so it preserves the squared Euclidean length a^2+b^2.
The zero initial state gives the stationary zero solution. Complex
eigenvectors are not arrows in this real state plane. Euler's formula
recombines the two complex modes into the real circular motion.
An exercise extension: start from a=2,b=-1 and recover the previously
computed coefficients 1+i/2 and 1-i/2; check y(0)=2 and y'(0)=-1.
:::

## Compare discrete steps and continuous time {#compare-discrete-steps-and-continuous-time}

### Example: a two-group population exchange {#a-two-group-population-exchange}

Each step: 20% of group 1 moves to group 2; 30% of group 2 moves to group 1

$$
\vct{x}_{k+1}=\mat{A}\vct{x}_k,\qquad
\mat{A}=\begin{bmatrix}0.8&0.3\\0.2&0.7\end{bmatrix},\qquad
\vct{x}_0=\begin{bmatrix}100\\0\end{bmatrix}
$$

Columns describe where each group's population goes; each column sums to 1

$$
p_{\mat{A}}(\lambda)=\lambda^2-1.5\lambda+0.5
=(\lambda-1)(\lambda-0.5)
$$

$$
\lambda_1=1:\ \vct{v}_1=\begin{bmatrix}3\\2\end{bmatrix},\qquad
\lambda_2=\tfrac12:\ \vct{v}_2=\begin{bmatrix}1\\-1\end{bmatrix}
$$

::: {.key-point}
One direction persists; the other describes a redistribution that decays
:::

::: {.notes}
This is a deterministic aggregate model (or expected counts); fractional
counts are allowed. There are no births or deaths, and transitions are
constant over time. The column convention matters: x is a column and
x_(k+1)=A x_k. The row [1,1] satisfies [1,1]A=[1,1], so total population
is conserved. The eigenvector v2 describes a signed perturbation, not
itself a nonnegative population. A v1=v1, A v2=(1/2)v2.
:::

---

### Separate the equilibrium from the changing part {#separate-the-equilibrium-from-the-changing-part}

Decompose the initial population into eigenvectors:

$$
\begin{bmatrix}100\\0\end{bmatrix}
=20\begin{bmatrix}3\\2\end{bmatrix}
+40\begin{bmatrix}1\\-1\end{bmatrix}
$$

Then

$$
\vct{x}_k
=20\begin{bmatrix}3\\2\end{bmatrix}
+40\left(\tfrac12\right)^k\begin{bmatrix}1\\-1\end{bmatrix}
=\begin{bmatrix}60+40(1/2)^k\\40-40(1/2)^k\end{bmatrix}
$$

$$
\vct{x}_1=\begin{bmatrix}80\\20\end{bmatrix},\qquad
\vct{x}_2=\begin{bmatrix}70\\30\end{bmatrix},\qquad
\vct{x}_k\longrightarrow\begin{bmatrix}60\\40\end{bmatrix}
$$

::: {.key-point}
The eigenvalue 1 gives the equilibrium proportions; $1/2$ gives the decay factor per step
:::

---

### Practice predicting discrete and continuous actions {#practice-predicting-repeated-actions}

::: {.exitem .lettered}
<span class="exbullet">$\exstar$</span>
<span>Use the eigenvectors to separate the scalar actions
<span class="exsub">For the population matrix, start with $[0,100]^\top$; find $\vct{x}_k$ and its limit</span>
<span class="exsub">For $\mat{A}=\begin{bmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{bmatrix}$ and $\vct{x}_0=[1,0]^\top$, find $\mat{A}^k\vct{x}_0$</span>
<span class="exsub">For that same $\mat{A}$, why does $\vct{x}_0=[1,-1]^\top$ stay fixed even though 3 is an eigenvalue?</span>
<span class="exsub">For that same $\mat{A}$, solve $\vct{x}'=\mat{A}\vct{x}$ from $\vct{x}(0)=[1,-1]^\top$; compare with the discrete steps</span>
</span>
:::

::: {.notes}
Population: x0=20[3,2]^T-60[1,-1]^T, so xk=[60-60(1/2)^k,
40+60(1/2)^k]^T and the limit is [60,40]^T. For the symmetric
matrix, e1=(v1+v2)/2, so A^k e1=[(3^k+1)/2,(3^k-1)/2]^T.
For x0=v2 the v1 coefficient is zero, so no growing component is present.
At k=0 the formula returns e1, and k=1 gives [2,1]^T.
For the differential system with x(0)=v2, x(t)=e^t v2 since lambda2=1;
the discrete system instead has A^k v2=1^k v2=v2. The same eigenvalue is
a per-step multiplier in one model and an exponential rate in the other.
:::

# Symmetric Matrices {#symmetric-matrices}

Symmetry guarantees a real eigenbasis with especially simple geometry

- [Symmetry makes different eigenspaces perpendicular](#symmetry-makes-different-eigenspaces-perpendicular)
- [The spectral theorem supplies an orthonormal eigenbasis](#the-spectral-theorem-supplies-an-orthonormal-eigenbasis)
- [Example: normalize the eigenvectors](#normalize-the-eigenvectors)
- [Practice orthogonal diagonalization](#practice-orthogonal-diagonalization)

## Symmetry makes different eigenspaces perpendicular {#symmetry-makes-different-eigenspaces-perpendicular}

Let $\mat{A}=\mat{A}^\top$ be real, with
$\mat{A}\vct{u}=\lambda\vct{u}$ and $\mat{A}\vct{v}=\mu\vct{v}$

Symmetry lets the action move across the dot product:

$$
\lambda\vct{u}^\top\vct{v}
=(\mat{A}\vct{u})^\top\vct{v}
=\vct{u}^\top\mat{A}\vct{v}
=\mu\vct{u}^\top\vct{v}
$$

Thus

$$
(\lambda-\mu)\vct{u}^\top\vct{v}=0
$$

::: {.key-point}
Distinct eigenvalues of a real symmetric matrix have perpendicular eigenvectors

&nbsp;

Within a repeated eigenspace, perpendicular basis vectors must still be chosen
:::

::: {.notes}
The displayed calculation concerns real eigenvectors and eigenvalues. The
spectral theorem on the next slide supplies their existence for all real
symmetric matrices. For a general nonsymmetric matrix, distinct eigenvalues
still imply independence but do not imply perpendicular eigenvectors: B in
the earlier exercise has eigenvectors [1,0]^T and [1,-2]^T. In a repeated
eigenspace every linear combination remains an eigenvector; therefore
Gram-Schmidt within that eigenspace, introduced in Inner Products, can
choose an orthonormal basis without changing the eigenvalue.
:::

## The spectral theorem supplies an orthonormal eigenbasis {#the-spectral-theorem-supplies-an-orthonormal-eigenbasis}

[Spectral theorem]{.alert}: every real symmetric matrix is [orthogonally diagonalizable]{.alert}

It has a real orthonormal eigenbasis

Put its unit eigenvectors in $\mat{Q}$, in the same order as $\mat{D}$:

$$
\mat{Q}^\top\mat{Q}=\mat{I},\qquad
\mat{Q}^{-1}=\mat{Q}^\top,\qquad
\boxed{\mat{A}=\mat{Q}\mat{D}\mat{Q}^\top}
$$

- All eigenvalues are real; repeated eigenvalues are allowed
- Coordinates are dot products: $[\vct{x}]_{\mathcal{Q}}=\mat{Q}^\top\vct{x}$
- Euclidean lengths are preserved: $\|\mat{Q}^\top\vct{x}\|=\|\vct{x}\|$

::: {.key-point}
A real matrix is orthogonally diagonalizable exactly when it is symmetric
:::

::: {.notes}
State the existence part as a theorem; the preceding orthogonality calculation
alone does not prove it. One proof selects a real unit eigenvector by
maximizing x^T A x on the unit sphere, shows its perpendicular complement
is invariant, and uses induction. That proof needs tools beyond the current
course prerequisites and is not required here. Conversely, Q D Q^T with
real diagonal D is symmetric by taking its transpose. Length preservation
follows by squaring the norm and using QQ^T=I. This strengthens the general
coordinate isomorphism, which preserves algebra but need not preserve
ordinary coordinate lengths. Repeated eigenspaces admit orthonormal bases.
:::

## Example: normalize the eigenvectors {#normalize-the-eigenvectors}

For $\mat{A}=\begin{bmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{bmatrix}$:

$$
\vct{q}_1=\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\begin{bmatrix}1\\1\end{bmatrix},\qquad
\vct{q}_2=\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\begin{bmatrix}1\\-1\end{bmatrix},\qquad
\mat{Q}=\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\begin{bmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{bmatrix}
$$

$$
\mat{Q}^\top\mat{A}\mat{Q}=\begin{bmatrix}3&0\\0&1\end{bmatrix},\qquad
\mat{A}=3\vct{q}_1\vct{q}_1^\top+\vct{q}_2\vct{q}_2^\top
$$

Each $\vct{q}_j\vct{q}_j^\top\vct{x}$ projects onto one unit eigendirection

::: {.key-point}
Resolve the input into perpendicular components, then scale each by its eigenvalue
:::

[Later: {{< meta decks.d11.short_title >}} — quadratic forms and principal axes]({{< meta decks.d11.file >}}#symmetry-gives-orthogonal-eigenvectors)

::: {.notes}
The projection statement follows from q q^T x=(q^T x)q and ||q||=1,
using the Euclidean projection formula already taught. Expanding the two
rank-one matrices gives (3/2)[[1,1],[1,1]]+(1/2)[[1,-1],[-1,1]]=A.
The sum of the two orthogonal projectors is I. PCA uses eigenvectors of
a symmetric covariance matrix; estimation, centering, and choice of how
many directions to retain belong to the later application. Do not imply
that arbitrary nonsymmetric matrices admit orthonormal eigenvectors.
:::

## Practice orthogonal diagonalization {#practice-orthogonal-diagonalization}

$$
\mat{C}=\begin{bmatrix}5&2\\2&5\end{bmatrix},\qquad
\mat{B}=\begin{bmatrix}4&1\\0&2\end{bmatrix}
$$

::: {.exitem .lettered}
<span class="exbullet">$\exstar$</span>
<span>Distinguish an eigenbasis from an orthonormal eigenbasis
<span class="exsub">Find an orthogonal $\mat{Q}$ and diagonal $\mat{D}$ with $\mat{C}=\mat{Q}\mat{D}\mat{Q}^\top$</span>
<span class="exsub">Write $\mat{C}$ as a sum of scaled orthogonal projectors</span>
<span class="exsub">The matrix $\mat{B}$ is diagonalizable; can it be orthogonally diagonalized over $\reals$? Explain</span>
</span>
:::

::: {.notes}
C has eigenvalues 7,3 with unit eigenvectors q1=[1,1]^T/sqrt(2),
q2=[1,-1]^T/sqrt(2). Q has those columns and D=diag(7,3).
C=7q1q1^T+3q2q2^T. B is not symmetric, so the converse of the real
spectral theorem rules out orthogonal diagonalization. Its eigenspaces
span the plane but are not perpendicular. Scaling its eigenvectors
cannot change the nonzero angle between those lines to a right angle.
:::

# Big Ideas {#big-ideas data-state="goldborder"}

- Eigenvectors are nonzero vectors satisfying $\mat{A}\vct{v}=\lambda\vct{v}$
- Characteristic roots give eigenvalues; shifted null spaces give eigenspaces
- An eigenvector basis makes the matrix diagonal
- Distinct eigenvalues guarantee independence; repeated roots require an eigenspace count
- The scalar field matters: real matrices can have nonreal eigenvalues
- Matrix functions apply $f(\lambda_j)$ to each eigenbasis component
- Powers use $\lambda_j^k$; the differential system $\vct{x}'=\mat{A}\vct{x}$ uses $e^{t\lambda_j}$
- Initial data and whole solutions have the same coordinates in corresponding eigenvector and solution-mode bases
- Real symmetric matrices have real orthonormal eigenbases
